Under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(15):

Hold-harmless obligations from divorce are NOT dischargeable in Chapter 7. Period.

In Chapter 13, they ARE dischargeable at plan completion if paid through the plan (they get unsecured-claim treatment unless they also qualify as DSO).

This creates a planning asymmetry: a California debtor whose post-divorce debt load is driven by hold-harmless obligations to an ex may prefer Chapter 13 over Chapter 7. See bankruptcy timing and divorce.

One filing fee, one attorney, one set of schedules.

Clears joint debt so neither spouse carries it post-divorce.

Works only if both spouses agree and have compatible exemption strategies.

In community-property states like California, joint filing simplifies the community-creditor analysis.

Can complicate divorce timeline.

Retirement accounts (401(k), pension, IRA) divided via Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO) in divorce. Bankruptcy treatment:

Spousal debt liability: Debts in one spouse's name only typically that spouse's; joint debts survive against both.

Timing note: CO courts equitable-distribute; hold-harmless clauses bind ex-spouses but not creditors.

## Divorce and Debt in Delaware [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing
Source: https://divorceanddebt.org/states/delaware.html

← divorceanddebt.org home

Divorce and Debt in Delaware [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Delaware residents.

Marital Property Regime: Delaware

Delaware is an equitable distribution state. Marital property and debts are divided equitably (fairly, not necessarily equally) based on economic and non-economic contributions, length of marriage, and other factors. Separate-name debts are generally separate liability.

Regime: Equitable distribution

Spousal debt liability: Household debts presumed joint if benefiting marital lifestyle; separate debts remain separate.

Timing note: DE equitable distribution standard.

Joint Debt After Divorce in Delaware

The most important rule about divorce and debt in Delaware: a divorce decree allocates debt between the spouses as a matter of contract law, but does not bind the creditor. If you signed a credit-card agreement with your spouse and the decree says your ex pays it, the creditor can still pursue you if the ex defaults. The decree gives you a contract claim against the ex, enforceable in the divorce court - but the credit hit and collection pressure are still yours to manage.

Three common Delaware scenarios:

Joint credit card, decree assigns to spouse A, spouse A defaults. Creditor pursues both; spouse B sues spouse A for indemnification under the decree.

Mortgage, decree assigns house to spouse A. If the mortgage remains in both names, spouse B's credit is still on the line for payment history; refinance is the clean fix.

Car loan, decree assigns to spouse B. Same dynamic; refinance or pay-off clears the non-taking spouse.

See hold-harmless clauses and joint debt after divorce.

Domestic Support Obligations (DSO) in Delaware

Domestic Support Obligations are treated specially in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 101(14A). A DSO is a debt that is:

Owed to or recoverable by a spouse, former spouse, child, or a governmental unit.

In the nature of alimony, maintenance, or support (without regard to label).

Established by a separation agreement, divorce decree, property settlement, court order, or governmental determination.

DSOs are:

Not dischargeable in Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(5).

Not dischargeable in Chapter 13 except to extent paid through the plan; any arrears survive.

Priority unsecured claims under 11 U.S.C. Section 507(a)(1)(A) - paid first among unsecured claims in a Ch 7 asset case or Ch 13 plan.

Not subject to the automatic stay for collection from non-estate property (post-petition income) under 11 U.S.C. Section 362(b)(2).

Delaware child-support enforcement continues through bankruptcy without stay relief. See DSO priority and treatment.

Hold-Harmless vs True Dischargeable Debt

A hold-harmless obligation in a divorce decree - "Spouse A agrees to indemnify Spouse B for the Visa balance" - is itself a debt. In bankruptcy, the question is whether it is dischargeable.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(15):

Hold-harmless obligations from divorce are NOT dischargeable in Chapter 7. Period.

In Chapter 13, they ARE dischargeable at plan completion if paid through the plan (they get unsecured-claim treatment unless they also qualify as DSO).

This creates a planning asymmetry: a Delaware debtor whose post-divorce debt load is driven by hold-harmless obligations to an ex may prefer Chapter 13 over Chapter 7. See bankruptcy timing and divorce.

Delaware Filing Timing: Before, During, or After Divorce

For Delaware couples:

File Jointly Before Divorce

One filing fee, one attorney, one set of schedules.

Clears joint debt so neither spouse carries it post-divorce.

Works only if both spouses agree and have compatible exemption strategies.

In community-property states like CA/TX/etc., joint filing simplifies the community-creditor analysis.

File During Divorce (Chapter 7 or Ch 13)

Automatic stay halts non-DSO portions of divorce proceedings (property division); DSO-related portions continue.

Can complicate divorce timeline.

Sometimes strategic when one spouse needs the stay against aggressive creditor action.

File After Divorce

Divorce decree allocates debt between spouses; bankruptcy then addresses post-decree allocated debt plus any hold-harmless obligations.

Ch 13 preserves ability to pay post-divorce hold-harmless through plan.

Ch 7 leaves hold-harmless obligations intact (523(a)(15) nondischargeable).

See filing during divorce.

Delaware Credit Card Debt in Divorce

Credit card debt in Delaware divorce breaks down as:

Joint cards (both names on account). Both spouses liable to the creditor. Decree allocation is between-spouses contract only.

Individual cards with authorized-user spouse. Only the primary account-holder is liable to the creditor. Authorized users have no liability unless Delaware has unusual doctrine-of-necessaries reach.

Individual cards, other spouse unaware. Only primary account-holder liable.

Community property state treatment (Delaware). Not a community property state; individual-signer rules apply.

See credit card debt and divorce.

Retirement and Homestead in Delaware Divorce

Retirement accounts (401(k), pension, IRA) divided via Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO) in divorce. Bankruptcy treatment:

Pre-QDRO retirement - generally ERISA-exempt in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 541(c)(2).

Post-QDRO transfer - the receiving spouse's share is their asset; bankruptcy exemption analysis applies to the recipient.

Homestead in Delaware: the divorce court often awards the marital residence to one spouse. If that spouse later files bankruptcy, Delaware homestead exemption applies on whatever they keep. See Delaware exemptions.

Related Delaware Resources

Community property states

Marital debt division

DSO treatment

Hold-harmless clauses

Timing: before/during/after

Filing during divorce

Credit card debt and divorce

Joint debt after divorce

## Divorce and Debt in District of Columbia [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing
Source: https://divorceanddebt.org/states/district-of-columbia.html

← divorceanddebt.org home

Divorce and Debt in District of Columbia [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for District of Columbia residents.

Marital Property Regime: District of Columbia

District of Columbia is an equitable distribution state. Marital property and debts are divided equitably (fairly, not necessarily equally) based on economic and non-economic contributions, length of marriage, and other factors. Separate-name debts are generally separate liability.

Regime: Equitable distribution

Spousal debt liability: Joint debts survive against both.

Timing note: DC courts allocate in decree; creditors not bound by allocation.

Joint Debt After Divorce in District of Columbia

The most important rule about divorce and debt in District of Columbia: a divorce decree allocates debt between the spouses as a matter of contract law, but does not bind the creditor. If you signed a credit-card agreement with your spouse and the decree says your ex pays it, the creditor can still pursue you if the ex defaults. The decree gives you a contract claim against the ex, enforceable in the divorce court - but the credit hit and collection pressure are still yours to manage.

Mortgage, decree assigns house to spouse A. If the mortgage remains in both names, spouse B's credit is still on the line for payment history; refinance is the clean fix.

Car loan, decree assigns to spouse B. Same dynamic; refinance or pay-off clears the non-taking spouse.

See hold-harmless clauses and joint debt after divorce.

Owed to or recoverable by a spouse, former spouse, child, or a governmental unit.

In the nature of alimony, maintenance, or support (without regard to label).

Established by a separation agreement, divorce decree, property settlement, court order, or governmental determination.

Not dischargeable in Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(5).

Not dischargeable in Chapter 13 except to extent paid through the plan; any arrears survive.

Priority unsecured claims under 11 U.S.C. Section 507(a)(1)(A) - paid first among unsecured claims in a Ch 7 asset case or Ch 13 plan.

Not subject to the automatic stay for collection from non-estate property (post-petition income) under 11 U.S.C. Section 362(b)(2).

District of Columbia child-support enforcement continues through bankruptcy without stay relief. See DSO priority and treatment.

A hold-harmless obligation in a divorce decree - "Spouse A agrees to indemnify Spouse B for the Visa balance" - is itself a debt. In bankruptcy, the question is whether it is dischargeable.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(15):

Hold-harmless obligations from divorce are NOT dischargeable in Chapter 7. Period.

In Chapter 13, they ARE dischargeable at plan completion if paid through the plan (they get unsecured-claim treatment unless they also qualify as DSO).

This creates a planning asymmetry: a District of Columbia debtor whose post-divorce debt load is driven by hold-harmless obligations to an ex may prefer Chapter 13 over Chapter 7. See bankruptcy timing and divorce.

District of Columbia Filing Timing: Before, During, or After Divorce

For District of Columbia couples:

File Jointly Before Divorce

One filing fee, one attorney, one set of schedules.

Clears joint debt so neither spouse carries it post-divorce.

Works only if both spouses agree and have compatible exemption strategies.

In community-property states like CA/TX/etc., joint filing simplifies the community-creditor analysis.

File During Divorce (Chapter 7 or Ch 13)

Automatic stay halts non-DSO portions of divorce proceedings (property division); DSO-related portions continue.

Can complicate divorce timeline.

Sometimes strategic when one spouse needs the stay against aggressive creditor action.

File After Divorce

Divorce decree allocates debt between spouses; bankruptcy then addresses post-decree allocated debt plus any hold-harmless obligations.

Ch 13 preserves ability to pay post-divorce hold-harmless through plan.

Ch 7 leaves hold-harmless obligations intact (523(a)(15) nondischargeable).

See filing during divorce.

District of Columbia Credit Card Debt in Divorce

Credit card debt in District of Columbia divorce breaks down as:

Joint cards (both names on account). Both spouses liable to the creditor. Decree allocation is between-spouses contract only.

Individual cards with authorized-user spouse. Only the primary account-holder is liable to the creditor. Authorized users have no liability unless District of Columbia has unusual doctrine-of-necessaries reach.

Individual cards, other spouse unaware. Only primary account-holder liable.

Community property state treatment (District of Columbia). Not a community property state; individual-signer rules apply.

See credit card debt and divorce.

Retirement and Homestead in District of Columbia Divorce

Retirement accounts (401(k), pension, IRA) divided via Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO) in divorce. Bankruptcy treatment:

Pre-QDRO retirement - generally ERISA-exempt in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 541(c)(2).

Post-QDRO transfer - the receiving spouse's share is their asset; bankruptcy exemption analysis applies to the recipient.

Homestead in District of Columbia: the divorce court often awards the marital residence to one spouse. If that spouse later files bankruptcy, District of Columbia homestead exemption applies on whatever they keep. See District of Columbia exemptions.

## Divorce and Debt in Florida [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing
Source: https://divorceanddebt.org/states/florida.html

← divorceanddebt.org home

Divorce and Debt in Florida [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Florida residents.

Marital Property Regime: Florida

Florida is an equitable distribution state. Marital property and debts are divided equitably (fairly, not necessarily equally) based on economic and non-economic contributions, length of marriage, and other factors. Separate-name debts are generally separate liability.

Regime: Equitable distribution

Spousal debt liability: FL recognizes the doctrine of necessaries: one spouse may be liable for the other's necessary household expenses (food, medical, housing). Non-necessaries signed by only one spouse = separate.

Timing note: FL courts equitable-distribute; FL head-of-household wage exemption (Fla. Stat. 222.11) affects post-divorce collection.

Joint Debt After Divorce in Florida

The most important rule about divorce and debt in Florida: a divorce decree allocates debt between the spouses as a matter of contract law, but does not bind the creditor. If you signed a credit-card agreement with your spouse and the decree says your ex pays it, the creditor can still pursue you if the ex defaults. The decree gives you a contract claim against the ex, enforceable in the divorce court - but the credit hit and collection pressure are still yours to manage.

Three common Florida scenarios:

Joint credit card, decree assigns to spouse A, spouse A defaults. Creditor pursues both; spouse B sues spouse A for indemnification under the decree.

Mortgage, decree assigns house to spouse A. If the mortgage remains in both names, spouse B's credit is still on the line for payment history; refinance is the clean fix.

Car loan, decree assigns to spouse B. Same dynamic; refinance or pay-off clears the non-taking spouse.

See hold-harmless clauses and joint debt after divorce.

Domestic Support Obligations (DSO) in Florida

Domestic Support Obligations are treated specially in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 101(14A). A DSO is a debt that is:

Owed to or recoverable by a spouse, former spouse, child, or a governmental unit.

In the nature of alimony, maintenance, or support (without regard to label).

Established by a separation agreement, divorce decree, property settlement, court order, or governmental determination.

DSOs are:

Not dischargeable in Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(5).

Not dischargeable in Chapter 13 except to extent paid through the plan; any arrears survive.

Priority unsecured claims under 11 U.S.C. Section 507(a)(1)(A) - paid first among unsecured claims in a Ch 7 asset case or Ch 13 plan.

Not subject to the automatic stay for collection from non-estate property (post-petition income) under 11 U.S.C. Section 362(b)(2).

Florida child-support enforcement continues through bankruptcy without stay relief. See DSO priority and treatment.

Hold-Harmless vs True Dischargeable Debt

A hold-harmless obligation in a divorce decree - "Spouse A agrees to indemnify Spouse B for the Visa balance" - is itself a debt. In bankruptcy, the question is whether it is dischargeable.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(15):

Hold-harmless obligations from divorce are NOT dischargeable in Chapter 7. Period.

In Chapter 13, they ARE dischargeable at plan completion if paid through the plan (they get unsecured-claim treatment unless they also qualify as DSO).

This creates a planning asymmetry: a Florida debtor whose post-divorce debt load is driven by hold-harmless obligations to an ex may prefer Chapter 13 over Chapter 7. See bankruptcy timing and divorce.

Florida Federal Bankruptcy Data

Divorce and bankruptcy frequently intersect: a Florida debtor may file either before, during, or after divorce, each with different strategic implications. These FJC numbers show the Florida consumer bankruptcy volume in which divorce-related debts appear.

Numbers below are from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 46,008 bankruptcy cases from Florida's federal bankruptcy courts.

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Florida Filing Timing: Before, During, or After Divorce

For Florida couples:

File Jointly Before Divorce

One filing fee, one attorney, one set of schedules.

Clears joint debt so neither spouse carries it post-divorce.

Works only if both spouses agree and have compatible exemption strategies.

In community-property states like CA/TX/etc., joint filing simplifies the community-creditor analysis.

Automatic stay halts non-DSO portions of divorce proceedings (property division); DSO-related portions continue.

Can complicate divorce timeline.

Ch 13 preserves ability to pay post-divorce hold-harmless through plan.

Ch 7 leaves hold-harmless obligations intact (523(a)(15) nondischargeable).

Florida Credit Card Debt in Divorce

Credit card debt in Florida divorce breaks down as:

Joint cards (both names on account). Both spouses liable to the creditor. Decree allocation is between-spouses contract only.

Individual cards with authorized-user spouse. Only the primary account-holder is liable to the creditor. Authorized users have no liability unless Florida has unusual doctrine-of-necessaries reach.

Individual cards, other spouse unaware. Only primary account-holder liable.

Community property state treatment (Florida). Not a community property state; individual-signer rules apply.

See credit card debt and divorce.

Retirement accounts (401(k), pension, IRA) divided via Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO) in divorce. Bankruptcy treatment:

Pre-QDRO retirement - generally ERISA-exempt in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 541(c)(2).

Post-QDRO transfer - the receiving spouse's share is their asset; bankruptcy exemption analysis applies to the recipient.

Homestead in Florida: the divorce court often awards the marital residence to one spouse. If that spouse later files bankruptcy, Florida homestead exemption applies on whatever they keep. See Florida exemptions.

## Divorce and Debt in Georgia [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing
Source: https://divorceanddebt.org/states/georgia.html

← divorceanddebt.org home

Divorce and Debt in Georgia [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Georgia residents.

Marital Property Regime: Georgia

Georgia is an equitable distribution state. Marital property and debts are divided equitably (fairly, not necessarily equally) based on economic and non-economic contributions, length of marriage, and other factors. Separate-name debts are generally separate liability.

Regime: Equitable distribution

Spousal debt liability: Separate-name debts = separate; joint debts = joint.

Timing note: GA hold-harmless enforcement between ex-spouses via contempt.

Joint Debt After Divorce in Georgia

The most important rule about divorce and debt in Georgia: a divorce decree allocates debt between the spouses as a matter of contract law, but does not bind the creditor. Sometimes strategic when one spouse needs the stay against aggressive creditor action.

File After Divorce

Divorce decree allocates debt between spouses; bankruptcy then addresses post-decree allocated debt plus any hold-harmless obligations.

Ch 13 preserves ability to pay post-divorce hold-harmless through plan.

Ch 7 leaves hold-harmless obligations intact (523(a)(15) nondischargeable).

See filing during divorce.

Hawaii Credit Card Debt in Divorce

Credit card debt in Hawaii divorce breaks down as:

Joint cards (both names on account). Both spouses liable to the creditor. Decree allocation is between-spouses contract only.

Individual cards with authorized-user spouse. Only the primary account-holder is liable to the creditor. Authorized users have no liability unless Hawaii has unusual doctrine-of-necessaries reach.

Individual cards, other spouse unaware. Only primary account-holder liable.

Community property state treatment (Hawaii). Not a community property state; individual-signer rules apply.

See credit card debt and divorce.

Retirement and Homestead in Hawaii Divorce

Retirement accounts (401(k), pension, IRA) divided via Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO) in divorce. Bankruptcy treatment:

Pre-QDRO retirement - generally ERISA-exempt in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 541(c)(2).

Post-QDRO transfer - the receiving spouse's share is their asset; bankruptcy exemption analysis applies to the recipient.

Homestead in Hawaii: the divorce court often awards the marital residence to one spouse. If that spouse later files bankruptcy, Hawaii homestead exemption applies on whatever they keep. See Hawaii exemptions.

DSO treatment

## Divorce and Debt in Idaho [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing
Source: https://divorceanddebt.org/states/idaho.html

← divorceanddebt.org home

Divorce and Debt in Idaho [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Idaho residents.

Marital Property Regime: Idaho

Idaho is one of nine community property states. This materially changes how debts and assets are allocated in both bankruptcy and divorce. Debts incurred during marriage are generally community debts reachable by creditors against community property, regardless of which spouse signed.

Regime: COMMUNITY PROPERTY

Spousal debt liability: Post-marriage debt is community debt; creditors reach community property. Separate-property debt belongs to the incurring spouse.

Timing note: ID post-divorce debt is separate; pre-divorce debt allocation in decree doesn't bind creditors.

Joint Debt After Divorce in Idaho

The most important rule about divorce and debt in Idaho: a divorce decree allocates debt between the spouses as a matter of contract law, but does not bind the creditor. If you signed a credit-card agreement with your spouse and the decree says your ex pays it, the creditor can still pursue you if the ex defaults. The decree gives you a contract claim against the ex, enforceable in the divorce court - but the credit hit and collection pressure are still yours to manage.

Three common Idaho scenarios:

Joint credit card, decree assigns to spouse A, spouse A defaults. Creditor pursues both; spouse B sues spouse A for indemnification under the decree.

Mortgage, decree assigns house to spouse A. If the mortgage remains in both names, spouse B's credit is still on the line for payment history; refinance is the clean fix.

Car loan, decree assigns to spouse B. Same dynamic; refinance or pay-off clears the non-taking spouse.

See hold-harmless clauses and joint debt after divorce.

Domestic Support Obligations (DSO) in Idaho

Domestic Support Obligations are treated specially in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 101(14A). A DSO is a debt that is:

Owed to or recoverable by a spouse, former spouse, child, or a governmental unit.

In the nature of alimony, maintenance, or support (without regard to label).

Established by a separation agreement, divorce decree, property settlement, court order, or governmental determination.

DSOs are:

Not dischargeable in Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(5).

Not dischargeable in Chapter 13 except to extent paid through the plan; any arrears survive.

Priority unsecured claims under 11 U.S.C. Section 507(a)(1)(A) - paid first among unsecured claims in a Ch 7 asset case or Ch 13 plan.

Not subject to the automatic stay for collection from non-estate property (post-petition income) under 11 U.S.C. Section 362(b)(2).

Idaho child-support enforcement continues through bankruptcy without stay relief. See DSO priority and treatment.

Hold-Harmless vs True Dischargeable Debt

A hold-harmless obligation in a divorce decree - "Spouse A agrees to indemnify Spouse B for the Visa balance" - is itself a debt. In bankruptcy, the question is whether it is dischargeable.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(15):

Hold-harmless obligations from divorce are NOT dischargeable in Chapter 7. Period.

In Chapter 13, they ARE dischargeable at plan completion if paid through the plan (they get unsecured-claim treatment unless they also qualify as DSO).

This creates a planning asymmetry: a Idaho debtor whose post-divorce debt load is driven by hold-harmless obligations to an ex may prefer Chapter 13 over Chapter 7. See bankruptcy timing and divorce.

Idaho Filing Timing: Before, During, or After Divorce

For Idaho couples:

File Jointly Before Divorce

One filing fee, one attorney, one set of schedules.

Clears joint debt so neither spouse carries it post-divorce.

Works only if both spouses agree and have compatible exemption strategies.

In community-property states like Idaho, joint filing simplifies the community-creditor analysis.

File During Divorce (Chapter 7 or Ch 13)

Automatic stay halts non-DSO portions of divorce proceedings (property division); DSO-related portions continue.

Can complicate divorce timeline.

Sometimes strategic when one spouse needs the stay against aggressive creditor action.

File After Divorce

Divorce decree allocates debt between spouses; bankruptcy then addresses post-decree allocated debt plus any hold-harmless obligations.

Ch 13 preserves ability to pay post-divorce hold-harmless through plan.

Ch 7 leaves hold-harmless obligations intact (523(a)(15) nondischargeable).

See filing during divorce.

Idaho Credit Card Debt in Divorce

Credit card debt in Idaho divorce breaks down as:

Joint cards (both names on account). Both spouses liable to the creditor. Decree allocation is between-spouses contract only.

Individual cards with authorized-user spouse. Only the primary account-holder is liable to the creditor. Authorized users have no liability unless Idaho has unusual doctrine-of-necessaries reach.

Individual cards, other spouse unaware. Only primary account-holder liable.

Community property state treatment (Idaho). In Idaho, during-marriage credit card debt is community debt even if only one spouse signed - creditors reach community property.

See credit card debt and divorce.

Retirement and Homestead in Idaho Divorce

Retirement accounts (401(k), pension, IRA) divided via Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO) in divorce. Bankruptcy treatment:

Pre-QDRO retirement - generally ERISA-exempt in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 541(c)(2).

Post-QDRO transfer - the receiving spouse's share is their asset; bankruptcy exemption analysis applies to the recipient.

Homestead in Idaho: the divorce court often awards the marital residence to one spouse. If that spouse later files bankruptcy, Idaho homestead exemption applies on whatever they keep. See Idaho exemptions.

Related Idaho Resources

DSO treatment

Hold-harmless clauses

## Divorce and Debt in Illinois [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing
Source: https://divorceanddebt.org/states/illinois.html

← divorceanddebt.org home

Divorce and Debt in Illinois [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Illinois residents.

Marital Property Regime: Illinois

Illinois is an equitable distribution state. Marital property and debts are divided equitably (fairly, not necessarily equally) based on economic and non-economic contributions, length of marriage, and other factors. Separate-name debts are generally separate liability.

Regime: Equitable distribution

Spousal debt liability: Joint debts survive; one-spouse-signed debts typically that spouse's only.

Timing note: IL courts allocate in decree; hold-harmless enforced via contempt.

The most important rule about divorce and debt in Illinois: a divorce decree allocates debt between the spouses as a matter of contract law, but does not bind the creditor. The decree gives you a contract claim against the ex, enforceable in the divorce court - but the credit hit and collection pressure are still yours to manage.

Mortgage, decree assigns house to spouse A. If the mortgage remains in both names, spouse B's credit is still on the line for payment history; refinance is the clean fix.

Car loan, decree assigns to spouse B. Same dynamic; refinance or pay-off clears the non-taking spouse.

Clears joint debt so neither spouse carries it post-divorce.

Divorce and Debt in Kansas [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Kansas residents.

Three common Kansas scenarios:

Joint credit card, decree assigns to spouse A, spouse A defaults. Creditor pursues both; spouse B sues spouse A for indemnification under the decree.

Mortgage, decree assigns house to spouse A. If the mortgage remains in both names, spouse B's credit is still on the line for payment history; refinance is the clean fix.

Car loan, decree assigns to spouse B. Same dynamic; refinance or pay-off clears the non-taking spouse.

See hold-harmless clauses and joint debt after divorce.

Domestic Support Obligations (DSO) in Kansas

Domestic Support Obligations are treated specially in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 101(14A). A DSO is a debt that is:

Owed to or recoverable by a spouse, former spouse, child, or a governmental unit.

In the nature of alimony, maintenance, or support (without regard to label).

Established by a separation agreement, divorce decree, property settlement, court order, or governmental determination.

DSOs are:

Not dischargeable in Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(5).

Not dischargeable in Chapter 13 except to extent paid through the plan; any arrears survive.

Priority unsecured claims under 11 U.S.C. Section 507(a)(1)(A) - paid first among unsecured claims in a Ch 7 asset case or Ch 13 plan.

Not subject to the automatic stay for collection from non-estate property (post-petition income) under 11 U.S.C. Section 362(b)(2).

Kansas child-support enforcement continues through bankruptcy without stay relief. See DSO priority and treatment.

Hold-Harmless vs True Dischargeable Debt

A hold-harmless obligation in a divorce decree - "Spouse A agrees to indemnify Spouse B for the Visa balance" - is itself a debt. In bankruptcy, the question is whether it is dischargeable.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(15):

Hold-harmless obligations from divorce are NOT dischargeable in Chapter 7. Period.

In Chapter 13, they ARE dischargeable at plan completion if paid through the plan (they get unsecured-claim treatment unless they also qualify as DSO).

This creates a planning asymmetry: a Kansas debtor whose post-divorce debt load is driven by hold-harmless obligations to an ex may prefer Chapter 13 over Chapter 7. See bankruptcy timing and divorce.

Kansas Federal Bankruptcy Data

Divorce and bankruptcy frequently intersect: a Kansas debtor may file either before, during, or after divorce, each with different strategic implications. These FJC numbers show the Kansas consumer bankruptcy volume in which divorce-related debts appear.

Numbers below are from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 40,849 bankruptcy cases from Kansas's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCasesDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 718,67399.4%0.5%

Chapter 1322,17673.1%26.9%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Kansas Filing Timing: Before, During, or After Divorce

For Kansas couples:

File Jointly Before Divorce

One filing fee, one attorney, one set of schedules.

Clears joint debt so neither spouse carries it post-divorce.

Works only if both spouses agree and have compatible exemption strategies.

In community-property states like CA/TX/etc., joint filing simplifies the community-creditor analysis.

File During Divorce (Chapter 7 or Ch 13)

Automatic stay halts non-DSO portions of divorce proceedings (property division); DSO-related portions continue.

Can complicate divorce timeline.

Sometimes strategic when one spouse needs the stay against aggressive creditor action.

File After Divorce

Divorce decree allocates debt between spouses; bankruptcy then addresses post-decree allocated debt plus any hold-harmless obligations.

Ch 13 preserves ability to pay post-divorce hold-harmless through plan.

Ch 7 leaves hold-harmless obligations intact (523(a)(15) nondischargeable).

See filing during divorce.

Kansas Credit Card Debt in Divorce

Credit card debt in Kansas divorce breaks down as:

Joint cards (both names on account). Both spouses liable to the creditor. Decree allocation is between-spouses contract only.

Individual cards with authorized-user spouse. Only the primary account-holder is liable to the creditor. Authorized users have no liability unless Kansas has unusual doctrine-of-necessaries reach.

Individual cards, other spouse unaware. Only primary account-holder liable.

Community property state treatment (Kansas). Not a community property state; individual-signer rules apply.

See credit card debt and divorce.

Retirement and Homestead in Kansas Divorce

Retirement accounts (401(k), pension, IRA) divided via Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO) in divorce. Bankruptcy treatment:

Pre-QDRO retirement - generally ERISA-exempt in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 541(c)(2).

Post-QDRO transfer - the receiving spouse's share is their asset; bankruptcy exemption analysis applies to the recipient.

Homestead in Kansas: the divorce court often awards the marital residence to one spouse. If that spouse later files bankruptcy, Kansas homestead exemption applies on whatever they keep. See Kansas exemptions.

## Divorce and Debt in Kentucky [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing
Source: https://divorceanddebt.org/states/kentucky.html

← divorceanddebt.org home

Divorce and Debt in Kentucky [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Kentucky residents.

Marital Property Regime: Kentucky

Kentucky is an equitable distribution state. Marital property and debts are divided equitably (fairly, not necessarily equally) based on economic and non-economic contributions, length of marriage, and other factors. Separate-name debts are generally separate liability.

Regime: Equitable distribution

Spousal debt liability: Joint debts survive divorce.

Timing note: KY applies unique "all property is marital" presumption subject to rebuttal.

Joint Debt After Divorce in Kentucky

The most important rule about divorce and debt in Kentucky: a divorce decree allocates debt between the spouses as a matter of contract law, but does not bind the creditor. If you signed a credit-card agreement with your spouse and the decree says your ex pays it, the creditor can still pursue you if the ex defaults. The decree gives you a contract claim against the ex, enforceable in the divorce court - but the credit hit and collection pressure are still yours to manage.

Three common Kentucky scenarios:

Joint credit card, decree assigns to spouse A, spouse A defaults. Creditor pursues both; spouse B sues spouse A for indemnification under the decree.

Mortgage, decree assigns house to spouse A. If the mortgage remains in both names, spouse B's credit is still on the line for payment history; refinance is the clean fix.

Car loan, decree assigns to spouse B. Same dynamic; refinance or pay-off clears the non-taking spouse.

See hold-harmless clauses and joint debt after divorce.

Domestic Support Obligations (DSO) in Kentucky

Domestic Support Obligations are treated specially in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 101(14A). A DSO is a debt that is:

Owed to or recoverable by a spouse, former spouse, child, or a governmental unit.

In the nature of alimony, maintenance, or support (without regard to label).

Established by a separation agreement, divorce decree, property settlement, court order, or governmental determination.

DSOs are:

Not dischargeable in Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(5).

Not dischargeable in Chapter 13 except to extent paid through the plan; any arrears survive.

Priority unsecured claims under 11 U.S.C. Section 507(a)(1)(A) - paid first among unsecured claims in a Ch 7 asset case or Ch 13 plan.

Not subject to the automatic stay for collection from non-estate property (post-petition income) under 11 U.S.C. Section 362(b)(2).

Kentucky child-support enforcement continues through bankruptcy without stay relief. See DSO priority and treatment.

Hold-Harmless vs True Dischargeable Debt

A hold-harmless obligation in a divorce decree - "Spouse A agrees to indemnify Spouse B for the Visa balance" - is itself a debt. In bankruptcy, the question is whether it is dischargeable.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(15):

Hold-harmless obligations from divorce are NOT dischargeable in Chapter 7. Period.

In Chapter 13, they ARE dischargeable at plan completion if paid through the plan (they get unsecured-claim treatment unless they also qualify as DSO).

This creates a planning asymmetry: a Kentucky debtor whose post-divorce debt load is driven by hold-harmless obligations to an ex may prefer Chapter 13 over Chapter 7. See bankruptcy timing and divorce.

Kentucky Federal Bankruptcy Data

Divorce and bankruptcy frequently intersect: a Kentucky debtor may file either before, during, or after divorce, each with different strategic implications. These FJC numbers show the Kentucky consumer bankruptcy volume in which divorce-related debts appear.

For Kentucky couples:

File Jointly Before Divorce

One filing fee, one attorney, one set of schedules.

Clears joint debt so neither spouse carries it post-divorce.

Works only if both spouses agree and have compatible exemption strategies.

In community-property states like CA/TX/etc., joint filing simplifies the community-creditor analysis.

Can complicate divorce timeline.

Ch 13 preserves ability to pay post-divorce hold-harmless through plan.

Ch 7 leaves hold-harmless obligations intact (523(a)(15) nondischargeable).

See filing during divorce.

Kentucky Credit Card Debt in Divorce

Credit card debt in Kentucky divorce breaks down as:

Joint cards (both names on account). Both spouses liable to the creditor. Decree allocation is between-spouses contract only.

Community property state treatment (Kentucky). Not a community property state; individual-signer rules apply.

See credit card debt and divorce.

Retirement accounts (401(k), pension, IRA) divided via Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO) in divorce. Bankruptcy treatment:

## Divorce and Debt in Louisiana [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing
Source: https://divorceanddebt.org/states/louisiana.html

← divorceanddebt.org home

Divorce and Debt in Louisiana [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Louisiana residents.

Marital Property Regime: Louisiana

Louisiana is one of nine community property states. This materially changes how debts and assets are allocated in both bankruptcy and divorce. Debts incurred during marriage are generally community debts reachable by creditors against community property, regardless of which spouse signed.

Regime: COMMUNITY PROPERTY (civil law framework)

Spousal debt liability: Louisiana community property is under civil code (unique among US states); debts of the community are joint obligations of the spouses.

Timing note: LA divorce terminates the community; post-termination debts separate.

Joint Debt After Divorce in Louisiana

The most important rule about divorce and debt in Louisiana: a divorce decree allocates debt between the spouses as a matter of contract law, but does not bind the creditor. If you signed a credit-card agreement with your spouse and the decree says your ex pays it, the creditor can still pursue you if the ex defaults. The decree gives you a contract claim against the ex, enforceable in the divorce court - but the credit hit and collection pressure are still yours to manage.

Three common Louisiana scenarios:

Joint credit card, decree assigns to spouse A, spouse A defaults. Creditor pursues both; spouse B sues spouse A for indemnification under the decree.

Mortgage, decree assigns house to spouse A. If the mortgage remains in both names, spouse B's credit is still on the line for payment history; refinance is the clean fix.

Car loan, decree assigns to spouse B. Same dynamic; refinance or pay-off clears the non-taking spouse.

See hold-harmless clauses and joint debt after divorce.

Domestic Support Obligations (DSO) in Louisiana

Domestic Support Obligations are treated specially in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 101(14A). A DSO is a debt that is:

Owed to or recoverable by a spouse, former spouse, child, or a governmental unit.

In the nature of alimony, maintenance, or support (without regard to label).

Established by a separation agreement, divorce decree, property settlement, court order, or governmental determination.

DSOs are:

Not dischargeable in Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(5).

Not dischargeable in Chapter 13 except to extent paid through the plan; any arrears survive.

Priority unsecured claims under 11 U.S.C. Section 507(a)(1)(A) - paid first among unsecured claims in a Ch 7 asset case or Ch 13 plan.

Not subject to the automatic stay for collection from non-estate property (post-petition income) under 11 U.S.C. Section 362(b)(2).

Louisiana child-support enforcement continues through bankruptcy without stay relief. See DSO priority and treatment.

Hold-Harmless vs True Dischargeable Debt

A hold-harmless obligation in a divorce decree - "Spouse A agrees to indemnify Spouse B for the Visa balance" - is itself a debt. In bankruptcy, the question is whether it is dischargeable.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(15):

Hold-harmless obligations from divorce are NOT dischargeable in Chapter 7. Period.

In Chapter 13, they ARE dischargeable at plan completion if paid through the plan (they get unsecured-claim treatment unless they also qualify as DSO).

This creates a planning asymmetry: a Louisiana debtor whose post-divorce debt load is driven by hold-harmless obligations to an ex may prefer Chapter 13 over Chapter 7. See bankruptcy timing and divorce.

Louisiana Filing Timing: Before, During, or After Divorce

For Louisiana couples:

File Jointly Before Divorce

One filing fee, one attorney, one set of schedules.

Clears joint debt so neither spouse carries it post-divorce.

Works only if both spouses agree and have compatible exemption strategies.

In community-property states like Louisiana, joint filing simplifies the community-creditor analysis.

File During Divorce (Chapter 7 or Ch 13)

Automatic stay halts non-DSO portions of divorce proceedings (property division); DSO-related portions continue.

Can complicate divorce timeline.

Sometimes strategic when one spouse needs the stay against aggressive creditor action.

File After Divorce

Divorce decree allocates debt between spouses; bankruptcy then addresses post-decree allocated debt plus any hold-harmless obligations.

Ch 13 preserves ability to pay post-divorce hold-harmless through plan.

Ch 7 leaves hold-harmless obligations intact (523(a)(15) nondischargeable).

See filing during divorce.

Louisiana Credit Card Debt in Divorce

Credit card debt in Louisiana divorce breaks down as:

Joint cards (both names on account). Both spouses liable to the creditor. Decree allocation is between-spouses contract only.

Individual cards with authorized-user spouse. Only the primary account-holder is liable to the creditor. Authorized users have no liability unless Louisiana has unusual doctrine-of-necessaries reach.

Individual cards, other spouse unaware. Only primary account-holder liable.

Community property state treatment (Louisiana). In Louisiana, during-marriage credit card debt is community debt even if only one spouse signed - creditors reach community property.

See credit card debt and divorce.

Retirement and Homestead in Louisiana Divorce

Retirement accounts (401(k), pension, IRA) divided via Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO) in divorce. Bankruptcy treatment:

Pre-QDRO retirement - generally ERISA-exempt in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 541(c)(2).

Post-QDRO transfer - the receiving spouse's share is their asset; bankruptcy exemption analysis applies to the recipient.

Homestead in Louisiana: the divorce court often awards the marital residence to one spouse. If that spouse later files bankruptcy, Louisiana homestead exemption applies on whatever they keep. See Louisiana exemptions.

## Divorce and Debt in Massachusetts [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing
Source: https://divorceanddebt.org/states/massachusetts.html

← divorceanddebt.org home

Divorce and Debt in Massachusetts [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Massachusetts residents.

Marital Property Regime: Massachusetts

Massachusetts is an equitable distribution state. Marital property and debts are divided equitably (fairly, not necessarily equally) based on economic and non-economic contributions, length of marriage, and other factors. Separate-name debts are generally separate liability.

Regime: Equitable distribution

Spousal debt liability: Joint = joint; separate = separate. MA doctrine of necessaries may apply in limited circumstances.

Timing note: MA equitable distribution is broad - nearly all pre- and post-marriage assets in the pot.

Joint Debt After Divorce in Massachusetts

The most important rule about divorce and debt in Massachusetts: a divorce decree allocates debt between the spouses as a matter of contract law, but does not bind the creditor. If you signed a credit-card agreement with your spouse and the decree says your ex pays it, the creditor can still pursue you if the ex defaults. The decree gives you a contract claim against the ex, enforceable in the divorce court - but the credit hit and collection pressure are still yours to manage.

Three common Massachusetts scenarios:

Joint credit card, decree assigns to spouse A, spouse A defaults. Creditor pursues both; spouse B sues spouse A for indemnification under the decree.

Mortgage, decree assigns house to spouse A. If the mortgage remains in both names, spouse B's credit is still on the line for payment history; refinance is the clean fix.

Car loan, decree assigns to spouse B. Same dynamic; refinance or pay-off clears the non-taking spouse.

See hold-harmless clauses and joint debt after divorce.

Domestic Support Obligations (DSO) in Massachusetts

Domestic Support Obligations are treated specially in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 101(14A). A DSO is a debt that is:

Owed to or recoverable by a spouse, former spouse, child, or a governmental unit.

In the nature of alimony, maintenance, or support (without regard to label).

Established by a separation agreement, divorce decree, property settlement, court order, or governmental determination.

DSOs are:

Not dischargeable in Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(5).

Not dischargeable in Chapter 13 except to extent paid through the plan; any arrears survive.

Priority unsecured claims under 11 U.S.C. Section 507(a)(1)(A) - paid first among unsecured claims in a Ch 7 asset case or Ch 13 plan.

Not subject to the automatic stay for collection from non-estate property (post-petition income) under 11 U.S.C. Section 362(b)(2).

Massachusetts child-support enforcement continues through bankruptcy without stay relief. See DSO priority and treatment.

Hold-Harmless vs True Dischargeable Debt

A hold-harmless obligation in a divorce decree - "Spouse A agrees to indemnify Spouse B for the Visa balance" - is itself a debt. In bankruptcy, the question is whether it is dischargeable.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(15):

Hold-harmless obligations from divorce are NOT dischargeable in Chapter 7. Period.

In Chapter 13, they ARE dischargeable at plan completion if paid through the plan (they get unsecured-claim treatment unless they also qualify as DSO).

This creates a planning asymmetry: a Massachusetts debtor whose post-divorce debt load is driven by hold-harmless obligations to an ex may prefer Chapter 13 over Chapter 7. See bankruptcy timing and divorce.

Massachusetts Federal Bankruptcy Data

Divorce and bankruptcy frequently intersect: a Massachusetts debtor may file either before, during, or after divorce, each with different strategic implications. These FJC numbers show the Massachusetts consumer bankruptcy volume in which divorce-related debts appear.

Numbers below are from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,356 bankruptcy cases from Massachusetts's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCasesDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 71,29098.3%0.9%

Chapter 136659.1%40.9%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Massachusetts Filing Timing: Before, During, or After Divorce

For Massachusetts couples:

File Jointly Before Divorce

One filing fee, one attorney, one set of schedules.

Clears joint debt so neither spouse carries it post-divorce.

Works only if both spouses agree and have compatible exemption strategies.

In community-property states like CA/TX/etc., joint filing simplifies the community-creditor analysis.

File During Divorce (Chapter 7 or Ch 13)

Automatic stay halts non-DSO portions of divorce proceedings (property division); DSO-related portions continue.

Can complicate divorce timeline.

Sometimes strategic when one spouse needs the stay against aggressive creditor action.

File After Divorce

Divorce decree allocates debt between spouses; bankruptcy then addresses post-decree allocated debt plus any hold-harmless obligations.

Ch 13 preserves ability to pay post-divorce hold-harmless through plan.

Ch 7 leaves hold-harmless obligations intact (523(a)(15) nondischargeable).

See filing during divorce.

Massachusetts Credit Card Debt in Divorce

Credit card debt in Massachusetts divorce breaks down as:

Joint cards (both names on account). Both spouses liable to the creditor. Decree allocation is between-spouses contract only.

Individual cards with authorized-user spouse. Only the primary account-holder is liable to the creditor. Authorized users have no liability unless Massachusetts has unusual doctrine-of-necessaries reach.

Individual cards, other spouse unaware. Only primary account-holder liable.

Community property state treatment (Massachusetts). Not a community property state; individual-signer rules apply.

See credit card debt and divorce.

Retirement and Homestead in Massachusetts Divorce

Retirement accounts (401(k), pension, IRA) divided via Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO) in divorce. Bankruptcy treatment:

Pre-QDRO retirement - generally ERISA-exempt in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 541(c)(2).

Post-QDRO transfer - the receiving spouse's share is their asset; bankruptcy exemption analysis applies to the recipient.

Homestead in Massachusetts: the divorce court often awards the marital residence to one spouse. If that spouse later files bankruptcy, Massachusetts homestead exemption applies on whatever they keep. See Massachusetts exemptions.

Related Massachusetts Resources

Community property states

Marital debt division

DSO treatment

Hold-harmless clauses

Timing: before/during/after

Filing during divorce

Credit card debt and divorce

## Divorce and Debt in Mississippi [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing
Source: https://divorceanddebt.org/states/mississippi.html

Missouri Filing Timing: Before, During, or After Divorce

For Missouri couples:

File Jointly Before Divorce

One filing fee, one attorney, one set of schedules.

Clears joint debt so neither spouse carries it post-divorce.

Works only if both spouses agree and have compatible exemption strategies.

In community-property states like CA/TX/etc., joint filing simplifies the community-creditor analysis.

File During Divorce (Chapter 7 or Ch 13)

Automatic stay halts non-DSO portions of divorce proceedings (property division); DSO-related portions continue.

Can complicate divorce timeline.

Sometimes strategic when one spouse needs the stay against aggressive creditor action.

File After Divorce

Divorce decree allocates debt between spouses; bankruptcy then addresses post-decree allocated debt plus any hold-harmless obligations.

Ch 13 preserves ability to pay post-divorce hold-harmless through plan.

Ch 7 leaves hold-harmless obligations intact (523(a)(15) nondischargeable).

See filing during divorce.

Missouri Credit Card Debt in Divorce

Credit card debt in Missouri divorce breaks down as:

Joint cards (both names on account). Both spouses liable to the creditor. Decree allocation is between-spouses contract only.

Individual cards with authorized-user spouse. Only the primary account-holder is liable to the creditor. Authorized users have no liability unless Missouri has unusual doctrine-of-necessaries reach.

Individual cards, other spouse unaware. Only primary account-holder liable.

Community property state treatment (Missouri). Not a community property state; individual-signer rules apply.

See credit card debt and divorce.

Retirement and Homestead in Missouri Divorce

Retirement accounts (401(k), pension, IRA) divided via Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO) in divorce. Bankruptcy treatment:

Pre-QDRO retirement - generally ERISA-exempt in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 541(c)(2).

Post-QDRO transfer - the receiving spouse's share is their asset; bankruptcy exemption analysis applies to the recipient.

Homestead in Missouri: the divorce court often awards the marital residence to one spouse. If that spouse later files bankruptcy, Missouri homestead exemption applies on whatever they keep. See Missouri exemptions.

## Divorce and Debt in Montana [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing
Source: https://divorceanddebt.org/states/montana.html

← divorceanddebt.org home

Divorce and Debt in Montana [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Montana residents.

Marital Property Regime: Montana

Montana is an equitable distribution state. Marital property and debts are divided equitably (fairly, not necessarily equally) based on economic and non-economic contributions, length of marriage, and other factors. Separate-name debts are generally separate liability.

Regime: Equitable distribution

Spousal debt liability: Joint = joint; separate = separate.

Timing note: MT courts equitable-distribute.

Joint Debt After Divorce in Montana

The most important rule about divorce and debt in Montana: a divorce decree allocates debt between the spouses as a matter of contract law, but does not bind the creditor. If you signed a credit-card agreement with your spouse and the decree says your ex pays it, the creditor can still pursue you if the ex defaults. The decree gives you a contract claim against the ex, enforceable in the divorce court - but the credit hit and collection pressure are still yours to manage.

Three common Montana scenarios:

Joint credit card, decree assigns to spouse A, spouse A defaults. Creditor pursues both; spouse B sues spouse A for indemnification under the decree.

Mortgage, decree assigns house to spouse A. If the mortgage remains in both names, spouse B's credit is still on the line for payment history; refinance is the clean fix.

Car loan, decree assigns to spouse B. Same dynamic; refinance or pay-off clears the non-taking spouse.

See hold-harmless clauses and joint debt after divorce.

Domestic Support Obligations (DSO) in Montana

Domestic Support Obligations are treated specially in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 101(14A). A DSO is a debt that is:

Owed to or recoverable by a spouse, former spouse, child, or a governmental unit.

In the nature of alimony, maintenance, or support (without regard to label).

Established by a separation agreement, divorce decree, property settlement, court order, or governmental determination.

DSOs are:

Not dischargeable in Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(5).

Not dischargeable in Chapter 13 except to extent paid through the plan; any arrears survive.

Priority unsecured claims under 11 U.S.C. Section 507(a)(1)(A) - paid first among unsecured claims in a Ch 7 asset case or Ch 13 plan.

Not subject to the automatic stay for collection from non-estate property (post-petition income) under 11 U.S.C. Section 362(b)(2).

Montana child-support enforcement continues through bankruptcy without stay relief. See DSO priority and treatment.

Hold-Harmless vs True Dischargeable Debt

A hold-harmless obligation in a divorce decree - "Spouse A agrees to indemnify Spouse B for the Visa balance" - is itself a debt. In bankruptcy, the question is whether it is dischargeable.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(15):

Hold-harmless obligations from divorce are NOT dischargeable in Chapter 7. Period.

In Chapter 13, they ARE dischargeable at plan completion if paid through the plan (they get unsecured-claim treatment unless they also qualify as DSO).

This creates a planning asymmetry: a Montana debtor whose post-divorce debt load is driven by hold-harmless obligations to an ex may prefer Chapter 13 over Chapter 7. See bankruptcy timing and divorce.

Montana Filing Timing: Before, During, or After Divorce

For Montana couples:

File Jointly Before Divorce

One filing fee, one attorney, one set of schedules.

Clears joint debt so neither spouse carries it post-divorce.

Works only if both spouses agree and have compatible exemption strategies.

In community-property states like CA/TX/etc., joint filing simplifies the community-creditor analysis.

File During Divorce (Chapter 7 or Ch 13)

Automatic stay halts non-DSO portions of divorce proceedings (property division); DSO-related portions continue.

Can complicate divorce timeline.

Sometimes strategic when one spouse needs the stay against aggressive creditor action.

File After Divorce

Divorce decree allocates debt between spouses; bankruptcy then addresses post-decree allocated debt plus any hold-harmless obligations.

Ch 13 preserves ability to pay post-divorce hold-harmless through plan.

Ch 7 leaves hold-harmless obligations intact (523(a)(15) nondischargeable).

See filing during divorce.

Montana Credit Card Debt in Divorce

Credit card debt in Montana divorce breaks down as:

Joint cards (both names on account). Both spouses liable to the creditor. Decree allocation is between-spouses contract only.

Individual cards with authorized-user spouse. Only the primary account-holder is liable to the creditor. Authorized users have no liability unless Montana has unusual doctrine-of-necessaries reach.

Individual cards, other spouse unaware. Only primary account-holder liable.

Community property state treatment (Montana). Not a community property state; individual-signer rules apply.

See credit card debt and divorce.

Retirement and Homestead in Montana Divorce

Retirement accounts (401(k), pension, IRA) divided via Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO) in divorce. Bankruptcy treatment:

Pre-QDRO retirement - generally ERISA-exempt in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 541(c)(2).

Post-QDRO transfer - the receiving spouse's share is their asset; bankruptcy exemption analysis applies to the recipient.

Homestead in Montana: the divorce court often awards the marital residence to one spouse. If that spouse later files bankruptcy, Montana homestead exemption applies on whatever they keep. See Montana exemptions.

## Divorce and Debt in Nevada [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing
Source: https://divorceanddebt.org/states/nevada.html

← divorceanddebt.org home

Divorce and Debt in Nevada [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Nevada residents.

Marital Property Regime: Nevada

Nevada is one of nine community property states. This materially changes how debts and assets are allocated in both bankruptcy and divorce. Debts incurred during marriage are generally community debts reachable by creditors against community property, regardless of which spouse signed.

Regime: COMMUNITY PROPERTY

Spousal debt liability: Post-marriage debt is community; creditors reach community property. Separate-property debt belongs to incurring spouse only.

Timing note: NV divorce terminates community; post-divorce debts separate. NV homestead protects primary residence.

Joint Debt After Divorce in Nevada

The most important rule about divorce and debt in Nevada: a divorce decree allocates debt between the spouses as a matter of contract law, but does not bind the creditor. If you signed a credit-card agreement with your spouse and the decree says your ex pays it, the creditor can still pursue you if the ex defaults. The decree gives you a contract claim against the ex, enforceable in the divorce court - but the credit hit and collection pressure are still yours to manage.

Three common Nevada scenarios:

Joint credit card, decree assigns to spouse A, spouse A defaults. Creditor pursues both; spouse B sues spouse A for indemnification under the decree.

Mortgage, decree assigns house to spouse A. If the mortgage remains in both names, spouse B's credit is still on the line for payment history; refinance is the clean fix.

Car loan, decree assigns to spouse B. Same dynamic; refinance or pay-off clears the non-taking spouse.

In the nature of alimony, maintenance, or support (without regard to label).

Owed to or recoverable by a spouse, former spouse, child, or a governmental unit.

In the nature of alimony, maintenance, or support (without regard to label).

Established by a separation agreement, divorce decree, property settlement, court order, or governmental determination.

DSOs are:

Not dischargeable in Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(5).

Not dischargeable in Chapter 13 except to extent paid through the plan; any arrears survive.

Priority unsecured claims under 11 U.S.C. Section 507(a)(1)(A) - paid first among unsecured claims in a Ch 7 asset case or Ch 13 plan.

Not subject to the automatic stay for collection from non-estate property (post-petition income) under 11 U.S.C. Section 362(b)(2).

New Jersey child-support enforcement continues through bankruptcy without stay relief. See DSO priority and treatment.

Hold-Harmless vs True Dischargeable Debt

A hold-harmless obligation in a divorce decree - "Spouse A agrees to indemnify Spouse B for the Visa balance" - is itself a debt. In bankruptcy, the question is whether it is dischargeable.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(15):

Hold-harmless obligations from divorce are NOT dischargeable in Chapter 7. Period.

In Chapter 13, they ARE dischargeable at plan completion if paid through the plan (they get unsecured-claim treatment unless they also qualify as DSO).

This creates a planning asymmetry: a New Jersey debtor whose post-divorce debt load is driven by hold-harmless obligations to an ex may prefer Chapter 13 over Chapter 7. See bankruptcy timing and divorce.

New Jersey Federal Bankruptcy Data

Divorce and bankruptcy frequently intersect: a New Jersey debtor may file either before, during, or after divorce, each with different strategic implications. These FJC numbers show the New Jersey consumer bankruptcy volume in which divorce-related debts appear.

Numbers below are from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,580 bankruptcy cases from New Jersey's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCasesDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 752697.3%2.7%

Chapter 131,05431.0%68.8%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

New Jersey Filing Timing: Before, During, or After Divorce

For New Jersey couples:

File Jointly Before Divorce

One filing fee, one attorney, one set of schedules.

Clears joint debt so neither spouse carries it post-divorce.

Works only if both spouses agree and have compatible exemption strategies.

In community-property states like CA/TX/etc., joint filing simplifies the community-creditor analysis.

File During Divorce (Chapter 7 or Ch 13)

Automatic stay halts non-DSO portions of divorce proceedings (property division); DSO-related portions continue.

Can complicate divorce timeline.

Sometimes strategic when one spouse needs the stay against aggressive creditor action.

File After Divorce

Divorce decree allocates debt between spouses; bankruptcy then addresses post-decree allocated debt plus any hold-harmless obligations.

Ch 13 preserves ability to pay post-divorce hold-harmless through plan.

Ch 7 leaves hold-harmless obligations intact (523(a)(15) nondischargeable).

See filing during divorce.

New Jersey Credit Card Debt in Divorce

Credit card debt in New Jersey divorce breaks down as:

Joint cards (both names on account). Both spouses liable to the creditor. Decree allocation is between-spouses contract only.

Individual cards with authorized-user spouse. Only the primary account-holder is liable to the creditor. Authorized users have no liability unless New Jersey has unusual doctrine-of-necessaries reach.

Individual cards, other spouse unaware. Only primary account-holder liable.

Community property state treatment (New Jersey). Not a community property state; individual-signer rules apply.

See credit card debt and divorce.

Retirement and Homestead in New Jersey Divorce

Retirement accounts (401(k), pension, IRA) divided via Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO) in divorce. Bankruptcy treatment:

Pre-QDRO retirement - generally ERISA-exempt in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 541(c)(2).

Post-QDRO transfer - the receiving spouse's share is their asset; bankruptcy exemption analysis applies to the recipient.

Homestead in New Jersey: the divorce court often awards the marital residence to one spouse. If that spouse later files bankruptcy, New Jersey homestead exemption applies on whatever they keep. See New Jersey exemptions.

## Divorce and Debt in New Mexico [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing
Source: https://divorceanddebt.org/states/new-mexico.html

← divorceanddebt.org home

Divorce and Debt in New Mexico [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New Mexico residents.

Marital Property Regime: New Mexico

New Mexico is one of nine community property states. This materially changes how debts and assets are allocated in both bankruptcy and divorce. Debts incurred during marriage are generally community debts reachable by creditors against community property, regardless of which spouse signed.

Regime: COMMUNITY PROPERTY

Spousal debt liability: Post-marriage debt is community; creditors reach community assets. Separate debts separate.

Timing note: NM post-divorce debts separate; quasi-community rules for pre-move assets.

Joint Debt After Divorce in New Mexico

The most important rule about divorce and debt in New Mexico: a divorce decree allocates debt between the spouses as a matter of contract law, but does not bind the creditor. If you signed a credit-card agreement with your spouse and the decree says your ex pays it, the creditor can still pursue you if the ex defaults. The decree gives you a contract claim against the ex, enforceable in the divorce court - but the credit hit and collection pressure are still yours to manage.

Three common New Mexico scenarios:

Joint credit card, decree assigns to spouse A, spouse A defaults. Creditor pursues both; spouse B sues spouse A for indemnification under the decree.

Mortgage, decree assigns house to spouse A. If the mortgage remains in both names, spouse B's credit is still on the line for payment history; refinance is the clean fix.

Car loan, decree assigns to spouse B. Same dynamic; refinance or pay-off clears the non-taking spouse.

See hold-harmless clauses and joint debt after divorce.

Domestic Support Obligations (DSO) in New Mexico

Domestic Support Obligations are treated specially in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 101(14A). A DSO is a debt that is:

Owed to or recoverable by a spouse, former spouse, child, or a governmental unit.

In the nature of alimony, maintenance, or support (without regard to label).

Established by a separation agreement, divorce decree, property settlement, court order, or governmental determination.

DSOs are:

Not dischargeable in Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(5).

Not dischargeable in Chapter 13 except to extent paid through the plan; any arrears survive.

Priority unsecured claims under 11 U.S.C. Section 507(a)(1)(A) - paid first among unsecured claims in a Ch 7 asset case or Ch 13 plan.

Not subject to the automatic stay for collection from non-estate property (post-petition income) under 11 U.S.C. Section 362(b)(2).

New Mexico child-support enforcement continues through bankruptcy without stay relief. See DSO priority and treatment.

Hold-Harmless vs True Dischargeable Debt

A hold-harmless obligation in a divorce decree - "Spouse A agrees to indemnify Spouse B for the Visa balance" - is itself a debt. In bankruptcy, the question is whether it is dischargeable.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(15):

Hold-harmless obligations from divorce are NOT dischargeable in Chapter 7. Period.

In Chapter 13, they ARE dischargeable at plan completion if paid through the plan (they get unsecured-claim treatment unless they also qualify as DSO).

This creates a planning asymmetry: a New Mexico debtor whose post-divorce debt load is driven by hold-harmless obligations to an ex may prefer Chapter 13 over Chapter 7. See bankruptcy timing and divorce.

New Mexico Filing Timing: Before, During, or After Divorce

For New Mexico couples:

File Jointly Before Divorce

One filing fee, one attorney, one set of schedules.

Clears joint debt so neither spouse carries it post-divorce.

Works only if both spouses agree and have compatible exemption strategies.

In community-property states like New Mexico, joint filing simplifies the community-creditor analysis.

File During Divorce (Chapter 7 or Ch 13)

Automatic stay halts non-DSO portions of divorce proceedings (property division); DSO-related portions continue.

Can complicate divorce timeline.

Sometimes strategic when one spouse needs the stay against aggressive creditor action.

File After Divorce

Divorce decree allocates debt between spouses; bankruptcy then addresses post-decree allocated debt plus any hold-harmless obligations.

Ch 13 preserves ability to pay post-divorce hold-harmless through plan.

Ch 7 leaves hold-harmless obligations intact (523(a)(15) nondischargeable).

See filing during divorce.

New Mexico Credit Card Debt in Divorce

Credit card debt in New Mexico divorce breaks down as:

Joint cards (both names on account). Both spouses liable to the creditor. Decree allocation is between-spouses contract only.

Individual cards with authorized-user spouse. Only the primary account-holder is liable to the creditor. Authorized users have no liability unless New Mexico has unusual doctrine-of-necessaries reach.

Individual cards, other spouse unaware. Only primary account-holder liable.

Community property state treatment (New Mexico). In New Mexico, during-marriage credit card debt is community debt even if only one spouse signed - creditors reach community property.

See credit card debt and divorce.

Retirement and Homestead in New Mexico Divorce

Retirement accounts (401(k), pension, IRA) divided via Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO) in divorce. Bankruptcy treatment:

Pre-QDRO retirement - generally ERISA-exempt in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 541(c)(2).

Post-QDRO transfer - the receiving spouse's share is their asset; bankruptcy exemption analysis applies to the recipient.

Homestead in New Mexico: the divorce court often awards the marital residence to one spouse. If that spouse later files bankruptcy, New Mexico homestead exemption applies on whatever they keep. See New Mexico exemptions.

## Divorce and Debt in New York [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing
Source: https://divorceanddebt.org/states/new-york.html

← divorceanddebt.org home

Divorce and Debt in New York [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New York residents.

Marital Property Regime: New York

New York is an equitable distribution state. Marital property and debts are divided equitably (fairly, not necessarily equally) based on economic and non-economic contributions, length of marriage, and other factors. Separate-name debts are generally separate liability.

Regime: Equitable distribution

Spousal debt liability: Joint debts survive; separate-name debts typically separate. NY has doctrine of necessaries for medical debt.

Timing note: NY equitable distribution; post-divorce debts separate.

Joint Debt After Divorce in New York

The most important rule about divorce and debt in New York: a divorce decree allocates debt between the spouses as a matter of contract law, but does not bind the creditor. Car loan, decree assigns to spouse B. Same dynamic; refinance or pay-off clears the non-taking spouse.

Hold-harmless obligations from divorce are NOT dischargeable in Chapter 7. Period.

In Chapter 13, they ARE dischargeable at plan completion if paid through the plan (they get unsecured-claim treatment unless they also qualify as DSO).

One filing fee, one attorney, one set of schedules.

Clears joint debt so neither spouse carries it post-divorce.
