## Divorce and Debt in Ohio [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing
Source: https://divorceanddebt.org/states/ohio.html

← divorceanddebt.org home

Divorce and Debt in Ohio [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Ohio residents.

Marital Property Regime: Ohio

Ohio is an equitable distribution state. Marital property and debts are divided equitably (fairly, not necessarily equally) based on economic and non-economic contributions, length of marriage, and other factors. Separate-name debts are generally separate liability.

Regime: Equitable distribution

Spousal debt liability: Joint debts survive; one-spouse debts typically separate.

Timing note: OH allows post-decree QDROs for retirement division; debts allocated in decree.

Joint Debt After Divorce in Ohio

The most important rule about divorce and debt in Ohio: a divorce decree allocates debt between the spouses as a matter of contract law, but does not bind the creditor. If you signed a credit-card agreement with your spouse and the decree says your ex pays it, the creditor can still pursue you if the ex defaults. The decree gives you a contract claim against the ex, enforceable in the divorce court - but the credit hit and collection pressure are still yours to manage.

Three common Ohio scenarios:

Joint credit card, decree assigns to spouse A, spouse A defaults. Creditor pursues both; spouse B sues spouse A for indemnification under the decree.

Mortgage, decree assigns house to spouse A. If the mortgage remains in both names, spouse B's credit is still on the line for payment history; refinance is the clean fix.

Car loan, decree assigns to spouse B. Same dynamic; refinance or pay-off clears the non-taking spouse.

See hold-harmless clauses and joint debt after divorce.

Domestic Support Obligations (DSO) in Ohio

Domestic Support Obligations are treated specially in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 101(14A). A DSO is a debt that is:

Owed to or recoverable by a spouse, former spouse, child, or a governmental unit.

In the nature of alimony, maintenance, or support (without regard to label).

Established by a separation agreement, divorce decree, property settlement, court order, or governmental determination.

DSOs are:

Not dischargeable in Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(5).

Not dischargeable in Chapter 13 except to extent paid through the plan; any arrears survive.

Priority unsecured claims under 11 U.S.C. Section 507(a)(1)(A) - paid first among unsecured claims in a Ch 7 asset case or Ch 13 plan.

Not subject to the automatic stay for collection from non-estate property (post-petition income) under 11 U.S.C. Section 362(b)(2).

Ohio child-support enforcement continues through bankruptcy without stay relief. See DSO priority and treatment.

Hold-Harmless vs True Dischargeable Debt

A hold-harmless obligation in a divorce decree - "Spouse A agrees to indemnify Spouse B for the Visa balance" - is itself a debt. In bankruptcy, the question is whether it is dischargeable.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(15):

Hold-harmless obligations from divorce are NOT dischargeable in Chapter 7. Period.

In Chapter 13, they ARE dischargeable at plan completion if paid through the plan (they get unsecured-claim treatment unless they also qualify as DSO).

This creates a planning asymmetry: a Ohio debtor whose post-divorce debt load is driven by hold-harmless obligations to an ex may prefer Chapter 13 over Chapter 7. See bankruptcy timing and divorce.

Ohio Federal Bankruptcy Data

Divorce and bankruptcy frequently intersect: a Ohio debtor may file either before, during, or after divorce, each with different strategic implications. These FJC numbers show the Ohio consumer bankruptcy volume in which divorce-related debts appear.

Numbers below are from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 3,971 bankruptcy cases from Ohio's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCasesDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 73,53597.7%1.8%

Chapter 1343651.1%48.9%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Ohio Filing Timing: Before, During, or After Divorce

For Ohio couples:

File Jointly Before Divorce

One filing fee, one attorney, one set of schedules.

Clears joint debt so neither spouse carries it post-divorce.

Works only if both spouses agree and have compatible exemption strategies.

In community-property states like CA/TX/etc., joint filing simplifies the community-creditor analysis.

File During Divorce (Chapter 7 or Ch 13)

Automatic stay halts non-DSO portions of divorce proceedings (property division); DSO-related portions continue.

Can complicate divorce timeline.

Sometimes strategic when one spouse needs the stay against aggressive creditor action.

File After Divorce

Divorce decree allocates debt between spouses; bankruptcy then addresses post-decree allocated debt plus any hold-harmless obligations.

Ch 13 preserves ability to pay post-divorce hold-harmless through plan.

Ch 7 leaves hold-harmless obligations intact (523(a)(15) nondischargeable).

See filing during divorce.

Ohio Credit Card Debt in Divorce

Credit card debt in Ohio divorce breaks down as:

Joint cards (both names on account). Both spouses liable to the creditor. Decree allocation is between-spouses contract only.

Individual cards with authorized-user spouse. Only the primary account-holder is liable to the creditor. Authorized users have no liability unless Ohio has unusual doctrine-of-necessaries reach.

Individual cards, other spouse unaware. Only primary account-holder liable.

Community property state treatment (Ohio). Not a community property state; individual-signer rules apply.

See credit card debt and divorce.

Retirement and Homestead in Ohio Divorce

Retirement accounts (401(k), pension, IRA) divided via Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO) in divorce. Bankruptcy treatment:

Pre-QDRO retirement - generally ERISA-exempt in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 541(c)(2).

Post-QDRO transfer - the receiving spouse's share is their asset; bankruptcy exemption analysis applies to the recipient.

Homestead in Ohio: the divorce court often awards the marital residence to one spouse. If that spouse later files bankruptcy, Ohio homestead exemption applies on whatever they keep. See Ohio exemptions.

Related Ohio Resources

Community property states

Marital debt division

DSO treatment

Hold-harmless clauses

Timing: before/during/after

Filing during divorce

Credit card debt and divorce

Joint debt after divorce

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Oregon residents.

Spousal debt liability: Joint debts survive.

Oregon Filing Timing: Before, During, or After Divorce

For Oregon couples:

File Jointly Before Divorce

One filing fee, one attorney, one set of schedules.

Clears joint debt so neither spouse carries it post-divorce.

Works only if both spouses agree and have compatible exemption strategies.

In community-property states like CA/TX/etc., joint filing simplifies the community-creditor analysis.

Credit card debt in Oregon divorce breaks down as:

Joint cards (both names on account). Both spouses liable to the creditor. Decree allocation is between-spouses contract only.

Individual cards with authorized-user spouse. Only the primary account-holder is liable to the creditor. Authorized users have no liability unless Oregon has unusual doctrine-of-necessaries reach.

Individual cards, other spouse unaware. Only primary account-holder liable.

Community property state treatment (Oregon). Not a community property state; individual-signer rules apply.

## Divorce and Debt in Pennsylvania [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing
Source: https://divorceanddebt.org/states/pennsylvania.html

← divorceanddebt.org home

Divorce and Debt in Pennsylvania [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Pennsylvania residents.

Rhode Island Credit Card Debt in Divorce

Credit card debt in Rhode Island divorce breaks down as:

Joint cards (both names on account). Both spouses liable to the creditor. Decree allocation is between-spouses contract only.

Individual cards with authorized-user spouse. Only the primary account-holder is liable to the creditor. Authorized users have no liability unless Rhode Island has unusual doctrine-of-necessaries reach.

Individual cards, other spouse unaware. Only primary account-holder liable.

Community property state treatment (Rhode Island). Not a community property state; individual-signer rules apply.

See credit card debt and divorce.

Retirement and Homestead in Rhode Island Divorce

Retirement accounts (401(k), pension, IRA) divided via Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO) in divorce. Bankruptcy treatment:

Pre-QDRO retirement - generally ERISA-exempt in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 541(c)(2).

Post-QDRO transfer - the receiving spouse's share is their asset; bankruptcy exemption analysis applies to the recipient.

Homestead in Rhode Island: the divorce court often awards the marital residence to one spouse. If that spouse later files bankruptcy, Rhode Island homestead exemption applies on whatever they keep. See Rhode Island exemptions.

Related Rhode Island Resources

## Divorce and Debt in South Carolina [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing
Source: https://divorceanddebt.org/states/south-carolina.html

← divorceanddebt.org home

Divorce and Debt in South Carolina [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for South Carolina residents.

Marital Property Regime: South Carolina

South Carolina is an equitable distribution state. Marital property and debts are divided equitably (fairly, not necessarily equally) based on economic and non-economic contributions, length of marriage, and other factors. Separate-name debts are generally separate liability.

Regime: Equitable distribution

Spousal debt liability: Joint debts survive; doctrine of necessaries applies.

Timing note: SC equitable apportionment under SC Code 20-3-620.

Joint Debt After Divorce in South Carolina

The most important rule about divorce and debt in South Carolina: a divorce decree allocates debt between the spouses as a matter of contract law, but does not bind the creditor. If you signed a credit-card agreement with your spouse and the decree says your ex pays it, the creditor can still pursue you if the ex defaults. The decree gives you a contract claim against the ex, enforceable in the divorce court - but the credit hit and collection pressure are still yours to manage.

Three common South Carolina scenarios:

Joint credit card, decree assigns to spouse A, spouse A defaults. Creditor pursues both; spouse B sues spouse A for indemnification under the decree.

Mortgage, decree assigns house to spouse A. If the mortgage remains in both names, spouse B's credit is still on the line for payment history; refinance is the clean fix.

Car loan, decree assigns to spouse B. Same dynamic; refinance or pay-off clears the non-taking spouse.

See hold-harmless clauses and joint debt after divorce.

Domestic Support Obligations (DSO) in South Carolina

Domestic Support Obligations are treated specially in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 101(14A). A DSO is a debt that is:

Owed to or recoverable by a spouse, former spouse, child, or a governmental unit.

In the nature of alimony, maintenance, or support (without regard to label).

Established by a separation agreement, divorce decree, property settlement, court order, or governmental determination.

DSOs are:

Not dischargeable in Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(5).

Not dischargeable in Chapter 13 except to extent paid through the plan; any arrears survive.

Priority unsecured claims under 11 U.S.C. Section 507(a)(1)(A) - paid first among unsecured claims in a Ch 7 asset case or Ch 13 plan.

Not subject to the automatic stay for collection from non-estate property (post-petition income) under 11 U.S.C. Section 362(b)(2).

South Carolina child-support enforcement continues through bankruptcy without stay relief. See DSO priority and treatment.

Hold-Harmless vs True Dischargeable Debt

A hold-harmless obligation in a divorce decree - "Spouse A agrees to indemnify Spouse B for the Visa balance" - is itself a debt. In bankruptcy, the question is whether it is dischargeable.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(15):

Hold-harmless obligations from divorce are NOT dischargeable in Chapter 7. Period.

In Chapter 13, they ARE dischargeable at plan completion if paid through the plan (they get unsecured-claim treatment unless they also qualify as DSO).

This creates a planning asymmetry: a South Carolina debtor whose post-divorce debt load is driven by hold-harmless obligations to an ex may prefer Chapter 13 over Chapter 7. See bankruptcy timing and divorce.

South Carolina Federal Bankruptcy Data

Divorce and bankruptcy frequently intersect: a South Carolina debtor may file either before, during, or after divorce, each with different strategic implications. These FJC numbers show the South Carolina consumer bankruptcy volume in which divorce-related debts appear.

Numbers below are from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 635 bankruptcy cases from South Carolina's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCasesDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 7301n/an/a

Chapter 13334n/an/a

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

South Carolina Filing Timing: Before, During, or After Divorce

For South Carolina couples:

File Jointly Before Divorce

One filing fee, one attorney, one set of schedules.

Clears joint debt so neither spouse carries it post-divorce.

Works only if both spouses agree and have compatible exemption strategies.

In community-property states like CA/TX/etc., joint filing simplifies the community-creditor analysis.

File During Divorce (Chapter 7 or Ch 13)

Automatic stay halts non-DSO portions of divorce proceedings (property division); DSO-related portions continue.

Can complicate divorce timeline.

Sometimes strategic when one spouse needs the stay against aggressive creditor action.

File After Divorce

Divorce decree allocates debt between spouses; bankruptcy then addresses post-decree allocated debt plus any hold-harmless obligations.

Ch 13 preserves ability to pay post-divorce hold-harmless through plan.

Ch 7 leaves hold-harmless obligations intact (523(a)(15) nondischargeable).

See filing during divorce.

South Carolina Credit Card Debt in Divorce

Credit card debt in South Carolina divorce breaks down as:

Joint cards (both names on account). Both spouses liable to the creditor. Decree allocation is between-spouses contract only.

Individual cards with authorized-user spouse. Only the primary account-holder is liable to the creditor. Authorized users have no liability unless South Carolina has unusual doctrine-of-necessaries reach.

Individual cards, other spouse unaware. Only primary account-holder liable.

Community property state treatment (South Carolina). Not a community property state; individual-signer rules apply.

See credit card debt and divorce.

Retirement and Homestead in South Carolina Divorce

Retirement accounts (401(k), pension, IRA) divided via Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO) in divorce. Bankruptcy treatment:

Pre-QDRO retirement - generally ERISA-exempt in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 541(c)(2).

Post-QDRO transfer - the receiving spouse's share is their asset; bankruptcy exemption analysis applies to the recipient.

Homestead in South Carolina: the divorce court often awards the marital residence to one spouse. If that spouse later files bankruptcy, South Carolina homestead exemption applies on whatever they keep. See South Carolina exemptions.

## Divorce and Debt in Texas [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing
Source: https://divorceanddebt.org/states/texas.html

← divorceanddebt.org home

Divorce and Debt in Texas [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Texas residents.

Marital Property Regime: Texas

Texas is one of nine community property states. This materially changes how debts and assets are allocated in both bankruptcy and divorce. Debts incurred during marriage are generally community debts reachable by creditors against community property, regardless of which spouse signed.

Regime: COMMUNITY PROPERTY

Spousal debt liability: TX community property is particularly broad. All property acquired during marriage is presumptively community - including debts. Creditors reach community property even if only one spouse signed. TX homestead is unlimited and strongly protected.

Timing note: TX post-divorce debts separate; quasi-community rules for move-in debt.

Joint Debt After Divorce in Texas

The most important rule about divorce and debt in Texas: a divorce decree allocates debt between the spouses as a matter of contract law, but does not bind the creditor. Not dischargeable in Chapter 13 except to extent paid through the plan; any arrears survive.

Priority unsecured claims under 11 U.S.C. Section 507(a)(1)(A) - paid first among unsecured claims in a Ch 7 asset case or Ch 13 plan.

Not subject to the automatic stay for collection from non-estate property (post-petition income) under 11 U.S.C. Section 362(b)(2).

Utah child-support enforcement continues through bankruptcy without stay relief. See DSO priority and treatment.

Hold-Harmless vs True Dischargeable Debt

A hold-harmless obligation in a divorce decree - "Spouse A agrees to indemnify Spouse B for the Visa balance" - is itself a debt. In bankruptcy, the question is whether it is dischargeable.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(15):

Hold-harmless obligations from divorce are NOT dischargeable in Chapter 7. Period.

In Chapter 13, they ARE dischargeable at plan completion if paid through the plan (they get unsecured-claim treatment unless they also qualify as DSO).

This creates a planning asymmetry: a Utah debtor whose post-divorce debt load is driven by hold-harmless obligations to an ex may prefer Chapter 13 over Chapter 7. See bankruptcy timing and divorce.

Utah Filing Timing: Before, During, or After Divorce

For Utah couples:

File Jointly Before Divorce

One filing fee, one attorney, one set of schedules.

Clears joint debt so neither spouse carries it post-divorce.

Works only if both spouses agree and have compatible exemption strategies.

In community-property states like CA/TX/etc., joint filing simplifies the community-creditor analysis.

File During Divorce (Chapter 7 or Ch 13)

Automatic stay halts non-DSO portions of divorce proceedings (property division); DSO-related portions continue.

Can complicate divorce timeline.

Sometimes strategic when one spouse needs the stay against aggressive creditor action.

File After Divorce

Divorce decree allocates debt between spouses; bankruptcy then addresses post-decree allocated debt plus any hold-harmless obligations.

Ch 13 preserves ability to pay post-divorce hold-harmless through plan.

Ch 7 leaves hold-harmless obligations intact (523(a)(15) nondischargeable).

See filing during divorce.

Utah Credit Card Debt in Divorce

Credit card debt in Utah divorce breaks down as:

Joint cards (both names on account). Both spouses liable to the creditor. Decree allocation is between-spouses contract only.

Individual cards with authorized-user spouse. Only the primary account-holder is liable to the creditor. Authorized users have no liability unless Utah has unusual doctrine-of-necessaries reach.

Individual cards, other spouse unaware. Only primary account-holder liable.

Community property state treatment (Utah). Not a community property state; individual-signer rules apply.

See credit card debt and divorce.

Retirement and Homestead in Utah Divorce

Retirement accounts (401(k), pension, IRA) divided via Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO) in divorce. Bankruptcy treatment:

Pre-QDRO retirement - generally ERISA-exempt in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 541(c)(2).

Post-QDRO transfer - the receiving spouse's share is their asset; bankruptcy exemption analysis applies to the recipient.

Homestead in Utah: the divorce court often awards the marital residence to one spouse. If that spouse later files bankruptcy, Utah homestead exemption applies on whatever they keep. See Utah exemptions.

## Divorce and Debt in Vermont [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing
Source: https://divorceanddebt.org/states/vermont.html

← divorceanddebt.org home

Divorce and Debt in Vermont [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Vermont residents.

Marital Property Regime: Vermont

Vermont is an equitable distribution state. Marital property and debts are divided equitably (fairly, not necessarily equally) based on economic and non-economic contributions, length of marriage, and other factors. Separate-name debts are generally separate liability.

Regime: Equitable distribution

Spousal debt liability: Joint debts survive.

Timing note: VT 15 V.S.A. Section 751 governs equitable distribution.

Joint Debt After Divorce in Vermont

The most important rule about divorce and debt in Vermont: a divorce decree allocates debt between the spouses as a matter of contract law, but does not bind the creditor. If you signed a credit-card agreement with your spouse and the decree says your ex pays it, the creditor can still pursue you if the ex defaults. The decree gives you a contract claim against the ex, enforceable in the divorce court - but the credit hit and collection pressure are still yours to manage.

Three common Vermont scenarios:

Joint credit card, decree assigns to spouse A, spouse A defaults. Creditor pursues both; spouse B sues spouse A for indemnification under the decree.

Mortgage, decree assigns house to spouse A. If the mortgage remains in both names, spouse B's credit is still on the line for payment history; refinance is the clean fix.

Car loan, decree assigns to spouse B. Same dynamic; refinance or pay-off clears the non-taking spouse.

See hold-harmless clauses and joint debt after divorce.

Domestic Support Obligations (DSO) in Vermont

Domestic Support Obligations are treated specially in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 101(14A). A DSO is a debt that is:

Owed to or recoverable by a spouse, former spouse, child, or a governmental unit.

In the nature of alimony, maintenance, or support (without regard to label).

Established by a separation agreement, divorce decree, property settlement, court order, or governmental determination.

DSOs are:

Not dischargeable in Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(5).

Not dischargeable in Chapter 13 except to extent paid through the plan; any arrears survive.

Priority unsecured claims under 11 U.S.C. Section 507(a)(1)(A) - paid first among unsecured claims in a Ch 7 asset case or Ch 13 plan.

Not subject to the automatic stay for collection from non-estate property (post-petition income) under 11 U.S.C. Section 362(b)(2).

Vermont child-support enforcement continues through bankruptcy without stay relief. See DSO priority and treatment.

Hold-Harmless vs True Dischargeable Debt

A hold-harmless obligation in a divorce decree - "Spouse A agrees to indemnify Spouse B for the Visa balance" - is itself a debt. In bankruptcy, the question is whether it is dischargeable.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(15):

Hold-harmless obligations from divorce are NOT dischargeable in Chapter 7. Period.

In Chapter 13, they ARE dischargeable at plan completion if paid through the plan (they get unsecured-claim treatment unless they also qualify as DSO).

This creates a planning asymmetry: a Vermont debtor whose post-divorce debt load is driven by hold-harmless obligations to an ex may prefer Chapter 13 over Chapter 7. See bankruptcy timing and divorce.

Vermont Filing Timing: Before, During, or After Divorce

For Vermont couples:

File Jointly Before Divorce

One filing fee, one attorney, one set of schedules.

Clears joint debt so neither spouse carries it post-divorce.

Works only if both spouses agree and have compatible exemption strategies.

In community-property states like CA/TX/etc., joint filing simplifies the community-creditor analysis.

File During Divorce (Chapter 7 or Ch 13)

Automatic stay halts non-DSO portions of divorce proceedings (property division); DSO-related portions continue.

Can complicate divorce timeline.

Sometimes strategic when one spouse needs the stay against aggressive creditor action.

File After Divorce

Divorce decree allocates debt between spouses; bankruptcy then addresses post-decree allocated debt plus any hold-harmless obligations.

Ch 13 preserves ability to pay post-divorce hold-harmless through plan.

Ch 7 leaves hold-harmless obligations intact (523(a)(15) nondischargeable).

See filing during divorce.

Vermont Credit Card Debt in Divorce

Credit card debt in Vermont divorce breaks down as:

Joint cards (both names on account). Both spouses liable to the creditor. Decree allocation is between-spouses contract only.

Individual cards with authorized-user spouse. Only the primary account-holder is liable to the creditor. Authorized users have no liability unless Vermont has unusual doctrine-of-necessaries reach.

Individual cards, other spouse unaware. Only primary account-holder liable.

Community property state treatment (Vermont). Not a community property state; individual-signer rules apply.

See credit card debt and divorce.

Retirement and Homestead in Vermont Divorce

Retirement accounts (401(k), pension, IRA) divided via Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO) in divorce. Bankruptcy treatment:

Pre-QDRO retirement - generally ERISA-exempt in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 541(c)(2).

Post-QDRO transfer - the receiving spouse's share is their asset; bankruptcy exemption analysis applies to the recipient.

Homestead in Vermont: the divorce court often awards the marital residence to one spouse. If that spouse later files bankruptcy, Vermont homestead exemption applies on whatever they keep. See Vermont exemptions.

Spousal debt liability: Joint = joint; separate = separate; marital debts allocated in decree.

## Divorce and Debt in Washington [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing
Source: https://divorceanddebt.org/states/washington.html

← divorceanddebt.org home

Divorce and Debt in Washington [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Washington residents.

Marital Property Regime: Washington

Washington is one of nine community property states. This materially changes how debts and assets are allocated in both bankruptcy and divorce. Debts incurred during marriage are generally community debts reachable by creditors against community property, regardless of which spouse signed.

Regime: COMMUNITY PROPERTY

Spousal debt liability: Post-marriage debt is community debt; community creditors reach community property. Separate debts separate.

Timing note: WA divorce terminates community; post-divorce debts separate.

Joint Debt After Divorce in Washington

The most important rule about divorce and debt in Washington: a divorce decree allocates debt between the spouses as a matter of contract law, but does not bind the creditor. If you signed a credit-card agreement with your spouse and the decree says your ex pays it, the creditor can still pursue you if the ex defaults. The decree gives you a contract claim against the ex, enforceable in the divorce court - but the credit hit and collection pressure are still yours to manage.

Three common Washington scenarios:

Joint credit card, decree assigns to spouse A, spouse A defaults. Creditor pursues both; spouse B sues spouse A for indemnification under the decree.

Mortgage, decree assigns house to spouse A. If the mortgage remains in both names, spouse B's credit is still on the line for payment history; refinance is the clean fix.

Car loan, decree assigns to spouse B. Same dynamic; refinance or pay-off clears the non-taking spouse.

In the nature of alimony, maintenance, or support (without regard to label).

Established by a separation agreement, divorce decree, property settlement, court order, or governmental determination.

Not dischargeable in Chapter 13 except to extent paid through the plan; any arrears survive.

Not subject to the automatic stay for collection from non-estate property (post-petition income) under 11 U.S.C. Section 362(b)(2).

Hold-harmless obligations from divorce are NOT dischargeable in Chapter 7. Period.

In Chapter 13, they ARE dischargeable at plan completion if paid through the plan (they get unsecured-claim treatment unless they also qualify as DSO).

Washington Filing Timing: Before, During, or After Divorce

For Washington couples:

File Jointly Before Divorce

One filing fee, one attorney, one set of schedules.

Clears joint debt so neither spouse carries it post-divorce.

Works only if both spouses agree and have compatible exemption strategies.

In community-property states like Washington, joint filing simplifies the community-creditor analysis.

Joint cards (both names on account). Both spouses liable to the creditor. Decree allocation is between-spouses contract only.

Individual cards with authorized-user spouse. Only the primary account-holder is liable to the creditor. Authorized users have no liability unless Washington has unusual doctrine-of-necessaries reach.

Individual cards, other spouse unaware. Only primary account-holder liable.

Community property state treatment (Washington). In Washington, during-marriage credit card debt is community debt even if only one spouse signed - creditors reach community property.

## Divorce and Debt in Wisconsin [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing
Source: https://divorceanddebt.org/states/wisconsin.html

Divorce and Debt in Wisconsin [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Wisconsin residents.

Marital Property Regime: Wisconsin

Wisconsin is one of nine community property states. This materially changes how debts and assets are allocated in both bankruptcy and divorce. Debts incurred during marriage are generally community debts reachable by creditors against community property, regardless of which spouse signed.

Regime: COMMUNITY PROPERTY (marital property state under Wis. Stat. Ch. 766)

Spousal debt liability: WI is the only Midwestern community-property state (adopted 1986). Post-marriage debt is marital; creditors reach marital property.

Timing note: WI divorce terminates the marital property regime; post-divorce debts separate.

Joint Debt After Divorce in Wisconsin

The most important rule about divorce and debt in Wisconsin: a divorce decree allocates debt between the spouses as a matter of contract law, but does not bind the creditor. If you signed a credit-card agreement with your spouse and the decree says your ex pays it, the creditor can still pursue you if the ex defaults. The decree gives you a contract claim against the ex, enforceable in the divorce court - but the credit hit and collection pressure are still yours to manage.

Three common Wisconsin scenarios:

Joint credit card, decree assigns to spouse A, spouse A defaults. Creditor pursues both; spouse B sues spouse A for indemnification under the decree.

Mortgage, decree assigns house to spouse A. If the mortgage remains in both names, spouse B's credit is still on the line for payment history; refinance is the clean fix.

Car loan, decree assigns to spouse B. Same dynamic; refinance or pay-off clears the non-taking spouse.

See hold-harmless clauses and joint debt after divorce.

Domestic Support Obligations (DSO) in Wisconsin

Domestic Support Obligations are treated specially in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 101(14A). A DSO is a debt that is:

Owed to or recoverable by a spouse, former spouse, child, or a governmental unit.

In the nature of alimony, maintenance, or support (without regard to label).

Established by a separation agreement, divorce decree, property settlement, court order, or governmental determination.

DSOs are:

Not dischargeable in Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(5).

Not dischargeable in Chapter 13 except to extent paid through the plan; any arrears survive.

Priority unsecured claims under 11 U.S.C. Section 507(a)(1)(A) - paid first among unsecured claims in a Ch 7 asset case or Ch 13 plan.

Not subject to the automatic stay for collection from non-estate property (post-petition income) under 11 U.S.C. Section 362(b)(2).

Wisconsin child-support enforcement continues through bankruptcy without stay relief. See DSO priority and treatment.

Hold-Harmless vs True Dischargeable Debt

A hold-harmless obligation in a divorce decree - "Spouse A agrees to indemnify Spouse B for the Visa balance" - is itself a debt. In bankruptcy, the question is whether it is dischargeable.

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 523(a)(15):

Hold-harmless obligations from divorce are NOT dischargeable in Chapter 7. Period.

In Chapter 13, they ARE dischargeable at plan completion if paid through the plan (they get unsecured-claim treatment unless they also qualify as DSO).

This creates a planning asymmetry: a Wisconsin debtor whose post-divorce debt load is driven by hold-harmless obligations to an ex may prefer Chapter 13 over Chapter 7. See bankruptcy timing and divorce.

Wisconsin Federal Bankruptcy Data

Divorce and bankruptcy frequently intersect: a Wisconsin debtor may file either before, during, or after divorce, each with different strategic implications. These FJC numbers show the Wisconsin consumer bankruptcy volume in which divorce-related debts appear.

Numbers below are from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,541 bankruptcy cases from Wisconsin's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCasesDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 795399.4%0.4%

Chapter 1358848.1%51.9%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Wisconsin Filing Timing: Before, During, or After Divorce

For Wisconsin couples:

File Jointly Before Divorce

One filing fee, one attorney, one set of schedules.

Clears joint debt so neither spouse carries it post-divorce.

Works only if both spouses agree and have compatible exemption strategies.

In community-property states like Wisconsin, joint filing simplifies the community-creditor analysis.

File During Divorce (Chapter 7 or Ch 13)

Automatic stay halts non-DSO portions of divorce proceedings (property division); DSO-related portions continue.

Can complicate divorce timeline.

Sometimes strategic when one spouse needs the stay against aggressive creditor action.

File After Divorce

Divorce decree allocates debt between spouses; bankruptcy then addresses post-decree allocated debt plus any hold-harmless obligations.

Ch 13 preserves ability to pay post-divorce hold-harmless through plan.

Ch 7 leaves hold-harmless obligations intact (523(a)(15) nondischargeable).

See filing during divorce.

Wisconsin Credit Card Debt in Divorce

Credit card debt in Wisconsin divorce breaks down as:

Joint cards (both names on account). Both spouses liable to the creditor. Decree allocation is between-spouses contract only.

Individual cards with authorized-user spouse. Only the primary account-holder is liable to the creditor. Authorized users have no liability unless Wisconsin has unusual doctrine-of-necessaries reach.

Individual cards, other spouse unaware. Only primary account-holder liable.

Community property state treatment (Wisconsin). In Wisconsin, during-marriage credit card debt is community debt even if only one spouse signed - creditors reach community property.

See credit card debt and divorce.

Retirement and Homestead in Wisconsin Divorce

Retirement accounts (401(k), pension, IRA) divided via Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO) in divorce. Bankruptcy treatment:

Pre-QDRO retirement - generally ERISA-exempt in bankruptcy under 11 U.S.C. Section 541(c)(2).

Post-QDRO transfer - the receiving spouse's share is their asset; bankruptcy exemption analysis applies to the recipient.

Homestead in Wisconsin: the divorce court often awards the marital residence to one spouse. If that spouse later files bankruptcy, Wisconsin homestead exemption applies on whatever they keep. See Wisconsin exemptions.

## Divorce and Debt in Wyoming [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing
Source: https://divorceanddebt.org/states/wyoming.html

← divorceanddebt.org home

Divorce and Debt in Wyoming [2026]: Marital Property, DSO, and Bankruptcy Timing

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Wyoming residents.

Marital Property Regime: Wyoming

Wyoming is an equitable distribution state. Marital property and debts are divided equitably (fairly, not necessarily equally) based on economic and non-economic contributions, length of marriage, and other factors. Separate-name debts are generally separate liability.

Regime: Equitable distribution

Spousal debt liability: Joint debts survive.

Timing note: WY equitable distribution under WY Stat. 20-2-114.

Joint Debt After Divorce in Wyoming

The most important rule about divorce and debt in Wyoming: a divorce decree allocates debt between the spouses as a matter of contract law, but does not bind the creditor. The decree gives you a contract claim against the ex, enforceable in the divorce court - but the credit hit and collection pressure are still yours to manage.

Joint credit card, decree assigns to spouse A, spouse A defaults. Creditor pursues both; spouse B sues spouse A for indemnification under the decree.

Mortgage, decree assigns house to spouse A. If the mortgage remains in both names, spouse B's credit is still on the line for payment history; refinance is the clean fix.

Car loan, decree assigns to spouse B. Same dynamic; refinance or pay-off clears the non-taking spouse.

See hold-harmless clauses and joint debt after divorce.

Not subject to the automatic stay for collection from non-estate property (post-petition income) under 11 U.S.C. Section 362(b)(2).

For Wyoming couples:

One filing fee, one attorney, one set of schedules.

Clears joint debt so neither spouse carries it post-divorce.

Works only if both spouses agree and have compatible exemption strategies.

Community property state treatment (Wyoming). Not a community property state; individual-signer rules apply.

See credit card debt and divorce.
